source.citation: Gais, S., Lucas, B., & Born, J. (2006). Sleep after learning aids memory recall. Learning & Memory, 13(3), 259-262. Wider review: Rasch, B., & Born, J. (2013). About sleep's role in memory. Physiological Reviews, 93(2), 681-766.
source.finding: People who slept within a few hours of learning word material recalled more of it later than people who stayed awake that night, even after everyone had a recovery night's sleep before the test.
source.caveat: The 2006 experiments were small lab studies using word lists. The wider research consistently links sleep with memory, but that is not the same as showing a set amount of sleep adds marks in an exam. The script gives no advice on how much sleep anyone needs.

scenes.narration: Staying up late to revise can cost you the very thing you stayed up for.
Learning doesn't stop when you close the book. Researchers think memories get strengthened while you sleep.
In a 2006 study, people learned lists of words. Some slept within a few hours. Others stayed awake all night.
Two days later, the ones who slept had remembered more. Even after everyone caught up on sleep.
That was a small study. But the wider research points the same way.
Tonight, go over your hardest topic for ten minutes before bed. Then test yourself in the morning.
